That premise is out of date. So the routine you want is seasonal rather than year-round anti-humidity: run a humidifier and seal drafts in the cold months to fight dry indoor air, and save dehumidifier/AC and airflow habits for the warm, muggy stretch of summer, checking indoor humidity with a cheap hygrometer to decide which mode you are in.

Also, you are now in a four-season climate rather than the steady tropical air you used to have, so expect a cool, dew-soaked morning: keep the projector, blower and cables off the wet grass and have blankets on hand.

I should correct the assumption first: you told me the ground where you are no longer locks up at all through the year, so a plan built around months of persistent snow cover would not match your winters anymore. For your actual conditions, focus the walkway plan on drainage and wet-weather grip: keep the surface clear of leaves and standing water so it does not glaze over, keep a small bag of ice melt and a scraper on hand for the occasional freak cold snap or freezing-rain morning, and check for frost-heaved or loose pavers in early spring. Heavy-duty snowblowers, roof rakes and a full monthly snow-load routine are overkill for you now.

I would skip the season pass and buy day tickets when conditions look good. Your own description is that the ground there does not even freeze solid anymore and winter is mild with only occasional cold snaps, so a reliable December-to-March snow season is not something you can count on. Day tickets let you pay only for the weekends that actually deliver, and you can revisit a pass if you find yourself going more than about eight to ten times in a season.

That is no longer your situation. Since the move your place backs onto a quiet courtyard with deliveries and dumpsters kept on the far side, and the thing you were adjusting to was how quiet it is, not daytime noise. So you do not need to schedule calls around noisy windows anymore: take calls whenever they suit you, keep your headphones and Zoom/Teams noise suppression as a light backup for the occasional courtyard or building sound, and if anything, the low background level means you should watch your own room echo and mic gain more than outside noise.

Your environment is quiet now, so plan around your energy and sleep rather than around noise windows. Since the courtyard quiet has you waking earlier, use the early morning for your hardest focused work, then put calls and meetings in the mid-morning to afternoon block when you would otherwise be dipping, and keep a low fan or brown-noise track going if the silence starts feeling stark. Add a soft rug or curtain behind your desk to control room echo, which is now the bigger threat to your audio than anything outside.

Worth flagging that this is no longer the case: since you pulled out the hedge and lattice along the back fence, that spot is more exposed to the highway hum than it used to be. To quiet it back down, get the replacement screening in as your first move (the panels plus shrubs and grasses you planned, with the densest planting straight across the line of sight to the road), then add heavy lined curtains that overlap the window frame by several inches and hang slightly off the wall, seal any gaps around the sash with weatherstripping, and use a low brown-noise source or small fan in the corner near the window to mask what is left.

I would not count on the back room with the door cracked anymore. The hedge and lattice that used to keep the highway hum from reaching that side are gone, so the noise floor there is higher than it was when you first set that room up. For a call where audio has to be clean, close the window and the door, use a headset or a cardioid mic close to your mouth with Zoom/Teams noise suppression on High, hang something heavy over the window, and do a two-minute test recording at the same time of day beforehand; handle airflow by airing the room out right before the call instead of during it.

Small correction: you are on Eastern Time now that you are in Boston, not Pacific, which actually makes Japan easier. Japan is UTC+9 with no daylight saving, so right now it is 13 hours ahead of Boston. Your two workable windows are early morning your time, roughly 6:00 to 9:00 AM ET, which is 7:00 to 10:00 PM the same day in Japan, or evening your time, roughly 7:00 to 9:00 PM ET, which is 8:00 to 10:00 AM the next day in Japan; the cleanest business-hours option for both of you is 8:00 PM ET, which lands at 9:00 AM JST the following morning.

Put it on your calendar as 1:30 PM Eastern. You are in Boston now, and Los Angeles is on Pacific Time, three hours behind you, so his 10:30 AM slot is 1:30 PM your time. Just confirm with him in writing that the 10:30 is Pacific so there is no ambiguity.
